question:
Let $g(x)=\csc^{-1}(2x-3)$.

(a) Determine the domain and range of $g$.

(b) Solve $g(x)=-\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

(c) Examine whether $0$ can be attained by $g$, giving a reason for your conclusion.
explanation:
(a)
For $\csc^{-1}(2x-3)$ to be defined,
$$|2x-3|\geq1$$
Therefore,
$$2x-3\leq-1\quad\text{or}\quad2x-3\geq1$$
This gives
$$x\leq1\quad\text{or}\quad x\geq2$$
Hence, the domain is
$$(-\infty,1]\cup[2,\infty)$$
The principal-value range of $\csc^{-1}t$ is
$$\left[-\frac{\pi}{2},0\right)\cup\left(0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right]$$
Therefore, this is also the range of $g$.

(b)
Given that
$$\csc^{-1}(2x-3)=-\frac{\pi}{6}$$
taking cosecant on both sides gives
$$2x-3=\csc\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=-2$$
Therefore,
$$2x=1$$
$$x=\frac{1}{2}$$
Since $\dfrac{1}{2}\leq1$, it belongs to the domain. Hence, $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$.

(c)
The value $0$ is excluded from the principal-value range of $\csc^{-1}t$. Equivalently, there is no real number whose cosecant is defined and equals an infinitely large value corresponding to an angle of $0$. Therefore, $g(x)$ cannot attain $0$ for any real value of $x$.
